prize_parts.citation: For the theoretical prediction of flat bands at a magic twist angle and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states in magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene, opening the field of moire quantum matter.

statement.case_for: My scientific case is unchanged, but I state it more narrowly after the first round. What I reward in B001 is two things that are established independently of the open questions: the Bistritzer-MacDonald continuum-model prediction (2011) that bands flatten at a magic angle, and the 2018 observation of correlated insulating and superconducting states at that angle. Both have been reproduced in many laboratories and carried over to other moire systems, where correlated and topological states are now seen in several different material platforms. A prediction made with a transparent model, tested in a material seven years later, and then extended well beyond the original system is the kind of loop between theory and measurement that I weigh most. It is also a field with no earlier prize, so a citation needs no argument about overlap. Electronic-structure theory can engage quantitatively with these systems, which tells me the results are not artefacts of one device. I accept that the chair's summary shows six colleagues preferring B007, and I have taken their arguments seriously. I still read them as reasons to treat B007 as a very strong alternative, not as reasons that make B001 weaker as science.
statement.case_against: The reservations I gave in round 1 stand and I do not want to play them down. The pairing mechanism of the superconductivity is unsettled, device-to-device variation from twist-angle disorder is real, and some correlated phases are still being assigned. The field is about eight years old. Credit is also awkward: Cao and the first experimental authors, groups such as Dean, Watanabe and Taniguchi, and earlier twisted-bilayer theory by Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto fall outside the three-name limit. Kroll and Olsson are right that the lattice clock has had two more decades of independent tests and has a cleaner two-name structure. Since the opening round I have also revised my own view of the overlap objection to B007: the chair's summary and my colleagues' replies show that the neutral-atom lattice clock is a distinct step from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, and that it has already produced physics (millimetre-scale redshift, bounds on varying constants, dark-matter limits). That weakens the main reason I ranked it fifth. What remains for me is category, not maturity: whether a clock invention should come before a new family of quantum states of matter. That is a judgement, not a defect in B007.

responses.point: Danielsson asked me which of the three B001 names I would remove if only two were possible, and whether the citation needs to name the 2011 prediction and the 2018 experiments separately. He also holds that the open pairing mechanism makes it risky to crown the field.
responses.response: The two-name question is not forced, because the rules allow three people and I would keep all three. If it were forced I would keep MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero and accept that this splits a joint 2011 calculation, which is exactly why I do not want to drop Bistritzer. Yes, the citation should name the magic-angle flat-band prediction and the 2018 correlated and superconducting states as two separate components, so that it does not claim all twisted-bilayer theory or the whole later field. On the mechanism, I accept your point that confirmation by many groups of the same phase diagram is not an explanation. But the committee has honoured discoveries whose origin was not understood at the time, and what B001 rewards is the existence of the phases at the predicted angle, which is settled. Where I concede ground to you is that the pairing question is a real reason for some members to prefer waiting, and I do not think it is unreasonable.

responses.point: Kroll holds that B001 is not obviously ahead of B007 on maturity or cleanliness of attribution: the pairing mechanism is debated, the first experimental authors are outside the names, and the lattice clocks have had two more decades of independent comparisons.
responses.response: On maturity and cleanliness of attribution I agree with you. B007 wins both, and I will not claim otherwise. I would add one distinction: the quantity that the clock community measures is stable and reproduced to a stated uncertainty, while for B001 what is stable is the phase diagram and not the explanation. That is a real difference. My reply is that maturity is not the only criterion. B001 is a discovery of new quantum behaviour in a material, predicted before it was seen, and a prize in the same year as the clock would need five names, which the rules do not allow. So the choice is a single part, and I do not think your maturity argument is wrong, only that it does not settle category. If the expert report confirms a clean priority record for Katori and Ye, I would regard B007 as an entirely legitimate prize and I would not oppose it.

responses.point: Olsson moved B007 ahead of twisted bilayer graphene after rereading the openings, mainly because the experimental claim is fully settled whereas the superconducting mechanism is not, and she wants the early lattice-clock papers checked before the committee commits.
responses.response: I agree that the historical record should be checked for B007 and the same should be done for B001. For the clock this means the first Katori proposal and realisation against Ye's strontium work and any early Lemonde contribution. For B001 it means confirming that the 2011 paper is the first quantitative prediction of a magic angle with flat bands, and that the 2018 papers are the first observation of the correlated and superconducting states, which I believe from memory but have not checked. I differ with you on one point. An experimental claim that is settled is a stronger argument for maturity than for being a discovery. Both of the 2018 observations are also settled as observations, and what remains open is the mechanism. Where you have persuaded me is that a prize on the strength of an untested priority history would be a mistake on either side, so I would accept the expert report as decisive for my final position.

responses.point: Mehlig reads B001 as a case where the mechanism is understood at the level of the essential model, and names B007 as the more mature and less contested choice if the committee finds the discovery not yet settled.
responses.response: I agree with your reading of the 2011 model, but I want the committee to state it carefully, because the continuum model explains the flat bands and the conditions for correlation, not the pairing glue. The citation should say that. I also take your fallback seriously and I share it: if the committee concludes that the superconducting phase is too unsettled, B007 is the right alternative, and I do not want my support to be read as resistance to it. Where I am slightly less confident than you is on the claim that the mechanism is understood. For the flat bands it is. For the superconductivity I would say the opposite, and I would not let the strength of the first argument carry over to the second.

uncertainties: How much weight the committee gives to the unresolved pairing mechanism and device-to-device variation when judging whether B001 is ready.

Whether three names are the fairest credit for B001, given Cao and the first experimental authors and earlier twisted-bilayer theory by Lopes dos Santos and colleagues. I rely on memory for the priority history and have not checked documents.
Whether the expert record on B007 supports Katori and Ye alone, and whether the lattice clock is judged a discovery of new measurement physics rather than an instrument advance.
Whether the pending redefinition of the second is a matter of maturity or only of timing for B007.
I defer to colleagues in atomic and precision physics on the details of the clock comparison record, since this is outside my own field.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict. My Uppsala group, Los Alamos collaborators, doctoral supervisor and monograph co-authors are not involved in any shortlisted candidate. I work in electronic-structure theory and magnetism, adjacent to the moire-materials community but not overlapping with it, and I flag that closeness so that colleagues can discount for it. I have no connection to Katori, Ye or the clock community.
